title: PostgreSQL Exception Handling in PL/pgSQL, With Examples
description: PostgreSQL exception handling in PL/pgSQL: catch errors with EXCEPTION WHEN, read SQLSTATE, log details and raise custom errors. Tested examples.

reviewNotes: Regular Saturday article (not a series part). Every SQL block was run in article order on a fresh database on PostgreSQL 18.7 (Ubuntu 18.7-1.pgdg24.04+2, PGDG packages) on Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS; followed the PostgreSQL 18 documentation (docs/current, pages in sources). Outputs are real; some outputs drop '(1 row)' lines and column headers for phone width (the withdraw output caption says so). SANDBOX CAVEAT: postgresql-18 depends on liburing2 from archive.ubuntu.com, which is blocked here, and installing a stub system package was not permitted this run. I extracted the official PGDG postgresql-18, postgresql-client-18 and libpq5 .deb files into a scratch directory and ran initdb/pg_ctl/psql from there with a stub liburing on LD_LIBRARY_PATH (server used the default io_method=worker). Same 18.7 binaries, so PL/pgSQL behaviour and messages are unaffected; no OS paths or service commands appear in the article. EDITOR CHECKS: (1) 'SQ001' is an invented custom SQLSTATE; the docs allow any five digits/upper-case letters except 00000 and advise against codes ending in 000. (2) The Oracle mapping table is from general Oracle knowledge, not the PostgreSQL docs (except the STRICT note, which the docs state matches Oracle). (3) The 'cannot commit while a subtransaction is active' and 'invalid transaction termination' messages were reproduced, not copied from docs. (4) Performance claim is the doc's own tip ('significantly more expensive'); no benchmark numbers given. Topic chosen from Google autocomplete ('postgresql exception handling', '... example', '... in function', 'plpgsql exception handling'); no existing article or draft covers it.

data.text: PostgreSQL exception handling in PL/pgSQL works with a BEGIN ... EXCEPTION WHEN ... THEN ... END block. When a statement inside the block fails, PostgreSQL stops running the block, undoes every change the block made, and runs the first WHEN handler that matches the error. If no handler matches, the error goes up to the caller as if the block had no exception section at all.

This tutorial shows every part of that with runnable examples on PostgreSQL 18: catching specific errors, reading SQLSTATE and SQLERRM, getting the constraint and table name with GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS, raising your own errors with RAISE EXCEPTION, and processing a batch where bad rows are logged instead of stopping the whole load. If you come from Oracle PL/SQL, there is a mapping table near the end.
How exception handling works in PL/pgSQL
Any PL/pgSQL block can have an EXCEPTION section. This is the general shape:

data.code:
[ DECLARE
    declarations ]
BEGIN
    statements
EXCEPTION
    WHEN condition [ OR condition ... ] THEN
        handler_statements
    [ WHEN condition [ OR condition ... ] THEN
        handler_statements ... ]
END;
data.caption: Syntax of a block with an exception handler

data.text: Four rules explain almost everything you will see in this article:

items.content: The block is undone, the variables are not. When an error is caught, all database changes made inside that block are rolled back, but local variables keep the values they had when the error happened.
The first matching handler wins. PostgreSQL checks the WHEN clauses from top to bottom and runs only the first one that matches.
Unmatched errors keep going. If no handler matches, the error moves to the enclosing block, then to the caller, and finally aborts the transaction.
An error inside a handler is not caught by the same handler. It goes out to an outer block, if there is one.

data.text: Under the hood, a block with an EXCEPTION section runs as a subtransaction. Think of it as an automatic savepoint: PostgreSQL marks a point when the block starts and rolls back to that mark when an error is caught. This is why PL/pgSQL has no SAVEPOINT command; a block with a handler does the same job.

The condition can be an error name such as unique_violation or division_by_zero, a five-character SQLSTATE code such as '23505', a whole category name such as integrity_constraint_violation, or OTHERS. Names are not case-sensitive. OTHERS matches every error except query_canceled and assert_failure.
Sample setup

Create a small payments schema in a scratch database. The balance_not_negative check constraint and the primary and foreign keys give us real errors to catch. audit_log and error_log are simple logging tables.

data.caption: Sample tables and data

data.code:
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 3
INSERT 0 1
data.caption: Output

data.text: Before writing any handler, find out which error code you need to catch. In psql, \set VERBOSITY verbose prints the SQLSTATE in front of every error message:

data.code:
\set VERBOSITY verbose
INSERT INTO payments VALUES (101, 2, 99.00);
data.caption: Show the SQLSTATE of an error in psql

data.code:
ERROR:  23505: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "payments_pkey"
DETAIL:  Key (payment_id)=(101) already exists.
SCHEMA NAME:  public
TABLE NAME:  payments
CONSTRAINT NAME:  payments_pkey
LOCATION:  _bt_check_unique, nbtinsert.c:666
data.caption: Output

data.text: Code 23505 is unique_violation. The full list of codes and names is in Appendix A of the PostgreSQL documentation ("PostgreSQL Error Codes"). The codes used in this article are:

content: Duplicate primary key or unique value
NULL in a NOT NULL column
Value too large for the numeric type
Bad argument (useful for your own errors)
SELECT INTO STRICT found no row

data.text: Type \set VERBOSITY default to go back to normal messages.
Catch a specific error
This function inserts a payment and turns the two errors we expect into friendly messages. Everything else is left alone on purpose.

data.caption: Handle unique_violation and foreign_key_violation

data.code:
add_payment
-------------------
 payment 102 saved

        add_payment
----------------------------
 payment 101 already exists

        add_payment
---------------------------
 account 99 does not exist
data.caption: Output

data.text: The first call succeeds. The second hits the primary key and the third hits the foreign key; both are caught and the function returns normally, so the caller's transaction carries on.
Now pass a NULL payment id. No handler matches a NOT NULL error, so it goes straight to the caller:

data.code: SELECT add_payment(NULL, 1, 50.00);
data.caption: An error with no matching handler

data.code:
ERROR:  null value in column "payment_id" of relation "payments" violates not-null constraint
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (null, 1, 50.00).
CONTEXT:  SQL statement "INSERT INTO payments (payment_id, account_id, amount)
  VALUES (p_id, p_account, p_amount)"
PL/pgSQL function add_payment(integer,integer,numeric) line 3 at SQL statement
data.caption: Output

data.text: This is the behaviour you want. Catch only the errors you know how to handle; let the rest fail loudly. The CONTEXT lines tell you the function and line number where the error happened.
What gets rolled back when an error is caught

This rule surprises many developers, so let us prove it. The function below writes an audit row in the outer block, then debits the account and records a payment in an inner block. The variable v_steps counts how many statements in the inner block finished.

data.caption: Inner block with a handler

data.code:
failed after 0 step(s): SQLSTATE 23514, new row for relation "accounts" violates check constraint "balance_not_negative"

 withdrawn 200.00

 failed after 1 step(s): SQLSTATE 23505, duplicate key value violates unique constraint "payments_pkey"
data.caption: Output (column headers removed)

data.text: Inside a handler, SQLSTATE holds the error code and SQLERRM holds the message. Look closely at the third call: the UPDATE worked (v_steps is 1), then the INSERT failed because payment 903 already existed. Now check the data:

data.code:
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts ORDER BY account_id;
SELECT note FROM audit_log ORDER BY log_id;
data.caption: Check what survived

data.code:
account_id | balance
------------+---------
          1 | 5000.00
          2 |  300.00
          3 | 1000.00
(3 rows)

              note
---------------------------------
 withdraw 1000.00 from account 2
 withdraw 200.00 from account 3
 withdraw 200.00 from account 3
(3 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Meera (account 3) has 1000.00: only the successful second call took money out. The debit from the third call was rolled back together with its failed insert, because both were in the inner block. The three audit rows survived because they were written in the outer block, before the inner block started. And the variable kept its value of 1, even though the update it counted was undone.
Put only the statements that must succeed or fail together inside the block with the handler. Anything you want to keep, such as an audit row, belongs outside it.
Get full error details with GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS

SQLSTATE and SQLERRM are often enough. When you need more, such as which constraint failed or the call stack, use GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS inside the handler. This function logs every failure with its details:

data.caption: Capture error details and log them

data.code:
NOTICE:  table=payments, detail=Key (account_id)=(7) is not present in table "accounts".
NOTICE:  context=SQL statement "INSERT INTO payments (payment_id, account_id, amount)
  VALUES (p_id, p_account, p_amount)"
PL/pgSQL function add_payment_logged(integer,integer,numeric) line 10 at SQL statement
 add_payment_logged
--------------------
 f

NOTICE:  table=, detail=A field with precision 12, scale 2 must round to an absolute value less than 10^10.
NOTICE:  context=SQL statement "INSERT INTO payments (payment_id, account_id, amount)
  VALUES (p_id, p_account, p_amount)"
PL/pgSQL function add_payment_logged(integer,integer,numeric) line 10 at SQL statement
 add_payment_logged
--------------------
 f
data.caption: Output

data.code: SELECT payment_id, sql_state, constraint_name, message FROM error_log ORDER BY error_id;
data.caption: The error log

content: insert or update on table "payments" violates foreign key constraint "payments_account_id_fkey"

data.text: The numeric overflow is not linked to a table or constraint, so TABLE_NAME and CONSTRAINT_NAME come back as empty strings, not NULL. The log rows were kept because the INSERT INTO error_log runs in the handler, after the block's own work was rolled back, and the function then returns normally.
The items you can read are:

content: The call stack where the error happened
The related data type, if any

data.text: Raise your own errors with RAISE EXCEPTION

Business rules need their own errors. RAISE EXCEPTION stops the code and aborts the transaction unless something catches it. Add USING to set the error code, a DETAIL line and a HINT. Without ERRCODE, the code is P0001.

data.caption: A procedure that raises its own errors

data.code:
ERROR:  insufficient funds in account 2
DETAIL:  balance 300.00, requested 500.00
HINT:  Reduce the amount or top up the account first.
CONTEXT:  PL/pgSQL function transfer(integer,integer,numeric) line 19 at RAISE
ERROR:  transfer amount must be positive, got -5
CONTEXT:  PL/pgSQL function transfer(integer,integer,numeric) line 6 at RAISE
ERROR:  account 42 not found
CONTEXT:  PL/pgSQL function transfer(integer,integer,numeric) line 14 at RAISE
data.caption: Output

data.text: Each % in the message is replaced by the next argument. SQ001 is a code we made up for "insufficient funds". PostgreSQL accepts any five characters made of digits and upper-case letters other than 00000; avoid codes ending in 000, because those are category codes. Applications can now react to SQ001 without parsing the message text.
Callers catch a custom code with WHEN SQLSTATE:

data.caption: Catch a custom SQLSTATE

data.code:
NOTICE:  caught: insufficient funds in account 2
DO
data.caption: Output

data.text: Levels below EXCEPTION (DEBUG, LOG, INFO, NOTICE, WARNING) only print a message and never stop the code. Whether you see them depends on client_min_messages and log_min_messages.
Re-raise an error with RAISE

Sometimes you want to do something when an error happens and still fail. A bare RAISE; inside a handler throws the same error again, with its original code and message. But watch what happens to the log row:

data.caption: Log and re-raise

data.code:
count
-------
     2

ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "payments_pkey"
DETAIL:  Key (payment_id)=(101) already exists.
CONTEXT:  SQL statement "INSERT INTO payments (payment_id, account_id, amount)
  VALUES (p_id, p_account, p_amount)"
PL/pgSQL function add_payment_strict(integer,integer,numeric) line 3 at SQL statement

 count
-------
     2
data.caption: Output

data.text: The count is still 2. The re-raised error aborted the caller's transaction, and the log insert was part of that transaction, so it was rolled back too. Logging inside the database and then failing does not leave a trace. If you must keep the log row, log from the application after the rollback, or return a status instead of re-raising. PostgreSQL has no autonomous transactions like Oracle's PRAGMA AUTONOMOUS_TRANSACTION.
Skip bad rows in a batch load
A common real job: load rows from a staging table, keep the good ones, and log the bad ones. Wrap each row in its own block so one bad row does not undo the others.

data.caption: One block per row

data.code:
NOTICE:  loaded 2, rejected 3
CALL
data.caption: Output

data.code:
SELECT payment_id, sql_state, message
  FROM error_log
 WHERE payment_id IN (101, 202, 204)
 ORDER BY error_id DESC
 LIMIT 3;
data.caption: Rows that were rejected

content: insert or update on table "payments" violates foreign key constraint "payments_account_id_fkey"
duplicate key value violates unique constraint "payments_pkey"

data.text: Payments 201 and 203 were loaded; the other three were logged with their reason. Note the OR that lets one handler cover several conditions. Any other error, such as a NOT NULL violation, still stops the whole load, which is usually what you want for an error you did not expect.

For a large load you may want to COMMIT as you go. In a procedure called with CALL, put the COMMIT outside the inner block, after END; and before END LOOP;. A COMMIT inside a block that has an EXCEPTION section fails, as the next section shows. To learn when to use a procedure rather than a function, see PostgreSQL function vs procedure.
Common mistakes
1. COMMIT inside a block with a handler

data.caption: This fails

data.code:
ERROR:  cannot commit while a subtransaction is active
CONTEXT:  PL/pgSQL function inline_code_block line 4 at COMMIT
data.caption: Output

data.text: The block is a subtransaction, so the transaction cannot end inside it. Move the COMMIT to a block without an EXCEPTION section. Also remember that transaction control works only in a CALL or DO run outside an explicit transaction: running CALL after BEGIN; gives ERROR: invalid transaction termination.
2. WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL
A handler that catches everything and does nothing hides real bugs: the function "succeeds" and the data is silently missing. Catch named conditions, or at least log SQLSTATE and SQLERRM.
3. Expecting OTHERS to catch a timeout

data.caption: OTHERS does not catch query_canceled

data.code:
ERROR:  canceling statement due to statement timeout
CONTEXT:  SQL statement "SELECT pg_sleep(5)"
PL/pgSQL function inline_code_block line 3 at PERFORM
data.caption: Output

data.text: OTHERS deliberately skips query_canceled so that a timeout or a cancel request from a DBA always stops your code. You can trap it by name, but that is rarely a good idea.
4. Using SQLERRM outside a handler

SQLSTATE and SQLERRM exist only inside an exception handler. Outside one, RAISE NOTICE '%', SQLERRM; fails with ERROR: column "sqlerrm" does not exist. Copy the values into your own variables in the handler if you need them later.
5. Expecting SELECT INTO to fail when no row is found
In Oracle, SELECT ... INTO raises NO_DATA_FOUND. In PL/pgSQL it does not: the variable is set to NULL and FOUND becomes false. Add STRICT to get the Oracle behaviour:

data.caption: SELECT INTO STRICT raises no_data_found

data.code:
owner_of |    owner_of
----------+-----------------
 Asha     | no such account
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: With STRICT, more than one row raises too_many_rows.
Oracle PL/SQL to PL/pgSQL mapping

content: EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN (does not catch query_canceled)
WHEN SQLSTATE '23505' or the condition name
A nested BEGIN ... EXCEPTION ... END block

data.text: Performance tips

items.content: The documentation warns that a block with an EXCEPTION clause is significantly more expensive to enter and exit than a block without one. Do not add a handler "just in case".
Check for expected conditions before they become errors. IF NOT FOUND after a plain SELECT INTO is cheaper than catching no_data_found.
For insert-or-update logic, use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT instead of catching unique_violation. The documentation itself recommends this; see PostgreSQL upsert with ON CONFLICT.

The row-by-row pattern above is fine for thousands of rows with occasional errors. For millions of clean rows, a single set-based INSERT ... SELECT is much faster; validate the data first and use the per-row loop only for the rows that fail.

data.text: Frequently asked questions
How do I catch all exceptions in PostgreSQL?
Use EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN. It catches every error except query_canceled and assert_failure. Always record SQLSTATE and SQLERRM in the handler so the error is not lost.
Does an exception roll back the whole transaction in PostgreSQL?
An uncaught error aborts the whole transaction. A caught error rolls back only the changes made inside the block that has the handler; work done before the block, in the same transaction, is kept.
How do I get the error message and line number in PL/pgSQL?
Inside the handler, SQLERRM gives the message. GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS v = PG_EXCEPTION_CONTEXT gives the call stack, including the function name and line number where the error happened.
What is the PostgreSQL equivalent of RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR?
RAISE EXCEPTION 'message' USING ERRCODE = 'SQ001', optionally with DETAIL and HINT. Without ERRCODE the error code is P0001.
Can I use exception handling in a plain SQL function?
No. LANGUAGE sql functions have no EXCEPTION section. Use LANGUAGE plpgsql, or a DO block for one-off scripts.
Summary

items.content: Wrap risky statements in BEGIN ... EXCEPTION WHEN ... THEN ... END; the first matching handler runs.
A caught error undoes the block's changes but keeps local variables and earlier work.
Find the code with \set VERBOSITY verbose and catch named conditions instead of OTHERS where you can.
Use SQLSTATE, SQLERRM and GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS to log what went wrong.
Raise business errors with RAISE EXCEPTION ... USING ERRCODE, DETAIL, HINT; re-raise with a bare RAISE;.
Remember that a re-raised error also rolls back any log row written in the handler.
Never COMMIT inside a block that has an EXCEPTION section, and add STRICT when you want SELECT INTO to fail on no rows.

linkedin.post:
A PL/pgSQL handler can log an error, re-raise it, and still lose the log row. Here is why.

PostgreSQL exception handling in 5 points:

→ A BEGIN ... EXCEPTION ... END block runs as a subtransaction. When an error is caught, every change made inside that block is undone, but local variables keep their values.

→ Find the code to catch with \set VERBOSITY verbose in psql. A duplicate key shows 23505, which you catch as WHEN unique_violation.

→ GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS gives you CONSTRAINT_NAME, TABLE_NAME, PG_EXCEPTION_DETAIL and the call stack, so your error log says exactly what failed.

→ RAISE EXCEPTION 'insufficient funds' USING ERRCODE = 'SQ001', HINT = '...' is the PL/pgSQL answer to RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR.

→ Coming from Oracle? SELECT INTO does not raise NO_DATA_FOUND unless you write SELECT INTO STRICT. And COMMIT inside a block with a handler fails with "cannot commit while a subtransaction is active".

Bonus: WHEN OTHERS does not catch a statement timeout. That is by design.

Which of these caught you out when moving from Oracle PL/SQL to PL/pgSQL?

Full tutorial with examples: link in the first comment.

slides.title: PostgreSQL Exception Handling
slides.body: Catch, log and raise errors in PL/pgSQL, with real output from PostgreSQL 18

slides.title: The basic block
points: The first matching WHEN handler runs
Unmatched errors go up to the caller

slides.title: What a caught error undoes
points: All changes made inside the block are rolled back
Work done before the block is kept

slides.title: Log the details
slides.code:
EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN
  GET STACKED DIAGNOSTICS
    v_state = RETURNED_SQLSTATE,
    v_cons  = CONSTRAINT_NAME,
    v_msg   = MESSAGE_TEXT;
  INSERT INTO error_log
  VALUES (v_state, v_cons, v_msg);

slides.title: Raise your own error
slides.code:
RAISE EXCEPTION 'insufficient funds %',
  p_from
  USING ERRCODE = 'SQ001',
        HINT = 'Top up first.';

slides.title: Traps for Oracle developers
points: SELECT INTO needs STRICT to raise no_data_found
No COMMIT inside a block with a handler
A re-raised error rolls back your log row too
WHEN OTHERS does not catch statement timeouts
